about.lead: I'm interested in how societies keep the lights on and the homes warm while moving to cleaner, fairer energy systems.
about.body:
## Hello, I'm [[Your Name]]

I'm a graduate student in the **Master of Sustainability** programme at the **University of Saskatchewan**, specialising in **Energy Security**. I started this site at the beginning of the programme because I learn best when I have to explain things — and because the questions I care about are better answered in conversation than alone.

## Academic background

[[Add your previous degree(s), the institution(s), and your year of graduation — for example: "BSc in (subject), (University), (Year)".]]

[[Optionally add one or two sentences on a thesis, capstone project or course that shaped your interest in energy.]]

## Professional background

[[Briefly describe your professional experience in two or three sentences — the sectors you've worked in, the kind of work you did, and what it taught you about energy systems. Only include what you're comfortable sharing publicly.]]

## Why sustainability and energy security?

Energy sits underneath almost everything — health, livelihoods, education, industry, and the way communities plan for the future. Yet the systems we rely on are being asked to change faster than at any point in living memory. I wanted to understand that change properly: not just the technologies, but the policies, institutions and people that decide whether a transition is secure, affordable and fair.

[[Add a personal sentence or two here about what drew you to this field — a moment, a place or an experience that made these questions feel real to you.]]

## What I hope to do with this

[[Describe your goals after the programme — for example, the kind of role, sector or research you're working towards.]]

## A note on this site

The views here are my own and reflect my learning as it happens. Some posts will be rough or incomplete, and I'll update them as my thinking changes. Where I draw on other people's work, I try to credit it clearly.

guidelines.title: Community guidelines
guidelines.body:
Thank you for taking the time to join the conversation. This is an academic learning space, and I want it to be welcoming for students, lecturers, practitioners and curious readers alike.

## How to take part

- **Be respectful.** Disagree with ideas, never with people. Personal attacks, harassment, discrimination or hateful language will be removed.
- **Bring evidence where you can.** Links to reports, papers or data are very welcome. Please say where a claim comes from.
- **Stay on topic.** Comments should relate to the post they're on.
- **Protect privacy.** Don't share personal information about yourself or anyone else.
- **No spam or advertising.** Promotional comments and unrelated links will not be published.
- **Be honest about who you are.** Use your real name or a consistent professional name. Affiliations are optional.

## How moderation works

- Every comment is reviewed before it appears. I aim to review new comments within [[number]] days.
- I don't edit what you write. If a comment doesn't meet these guidelines, I'll decline it rather than change it.
- Spam is filtered automatically, and submissions that look automated are discarded.
- Your email address is used only to verify your comment and, if needed, to contact you about it. It is never published.

## Removing a comment

If you'd like a comment you've posted removed, use the [contact form](#/contact) and I'll take it down.

## Academic integrity

Please don't post assignment answers or confidential course material. If you quote something, credit it.

privacy.title: Privacy notice
privacy.body:
This site collects as little personal information as possible.

## What is collected

- **Contact form:** your name, email address, optional affiliation and your message.
- **Comments:** your name, email address (never published), optional affiliation and your comment.
- **Email updates:** your email address, if you choose to subscribe.

## How it is used

Information is used only to reply to you, to moderate and publish comments, and to send the updates you asked for. It is not sold or shared for marketing.

## Where it is stored

Form submissions are stored by the website host, [[name your hosting provider, e.g. Netlify]]. If you subscribe, your email address is stored by [[name your email provider]].

## How long it is kept

[[State how long you keep messages, comments and subscriber details — for example, "until the end of my programme, then deleted".]]

## Your choices

You can unsubscribe at any time using the link in any email, or ask for your information to be corrected or deleted through the [contact form](#/contact).

## Cookies and analytics

This site does not use advertising or tracking cookies. Display preferences (such as text size) are saved only in your own browser.

*Last updated: [[date]]*

posts.title: Repurposing oil and gas infrastructure for cleaner energy
posts.excerpt: Working notes for an essay: can wells, pipelines, reservoirs and skills from the oil and gas sector help build a cleaner energy system — and what are the risks of doing so?
posts.body:
These are my working notes for an essay on repurposing oil and gas infrastructure. I'm sharing them early because I'd value challenge on the argument before I write the final version.

## The basic idea

Decades of oil and gas development have left behind a huge amount of physical infrastructure, geological knowledge and skilled people. Rather than treating all of it as a liability, could some of it be reused to support a cleaner energy system?

## Options I'm looking at

- **Geothermal energy.** Old wells and deep sedimentary formations can sometimes be used to access underground heat. Geothermal developers in southeast Saskatchewan have been exploring this kind of resource. [[Add source]]
- **Carbon capture and storage.** Depleted reservoirs and existing pipelines may be suitable for transporting and storing CO₂. SaskPower's Boundary Dam carbon capture project is a frequently discussed — and debated — example. [[Add source]]
- **Hydrogen.** Some pipelines may be able to carry hydrogen blends, though steel compatibility and safety need careful assessment.
- **People and skills.** Drilling, subsurface engineering, project management and safety cultures transfer well to geothermal, storage and other clean energy work.
- **Data and knowledge.** Seismic surveys and well records are valuable for understanding the subsurface for new uses.

## The risks and open questions

- **Technical integrity.** Old wells and pipelines weren't designed for these new uses. Testing and upgrades can be costly.
- **Liability.** Who is responsible if a repurposed well leaks — the original operator, the new one, or the public?
- **Lock-in.** Some uses, especially carbon capture tied to continued fossil fuel production, may extend reliance on fossil fuels rather than reduce it.
- **Economics.** Repurposing only makes sense if it is cheaper or better than building new.
- **Fairness.** Workers and communities in producing regions need a real stake in what comes next.

## My working argument

*Repurposing can be a valuable part of an energy transition when it reduces emissions and costs, transfers skills, and is backed by clear rules on liability — but it should be judged case by case, not used as a reason to delay change.*

[[Refine your thesis statement here and add your marker's feedback when you receive it.]]

## Key takeaways so far

> - Existing infrastructure and skills can be assets for the transition, not only liabilities.
> - Every repurposing option needs a clear-eyed look at integrity, liability and lock-in.
> - The strongest case is where repurposing also delivers local jobs and benefits.

*If you've worked on any of these technologies, I'd love to hear where my notes are wrong or incomplete.*

posts.title: Renewable energy, participation, ownership and energy justice
posts.excerpt: A wind farm can be clean and still feel unfair. Notes on why participation and ownership shape whether renewable energy projects deliver justice — and not just electricity.
posts.body:
One idea from this week's readings has stuck with me: *a project can be renewable and still be unjust.* This post pulls together my notes on why participation and ownership matter so much.

## Three ways of looking at energy justice

The readings this week used a framework with three tenets:

- **Distributional justice** — how the benefits (jobs, revenue, cheaper power) and burdens (land use, noise, visual impact, cost) are shared.
- **Procedural justice** — whether people affected by a decision have a fair and meaningful say in it.
- **Recognition justice** — whether different groups, knowledges and rights are acknowledged and respected.

[[Add citation — e.g. Jenkins et al. (2016)]]

## Participation is not the same as consultation

It's easy to tick a box by holding an information session after the key decisions are already made. Real participation starts earlier and gives people genuine influence — over the site, the scale, the design and how benefits are shared. Arnstein's well-known "ladder of participation" was a useful reminder that informing people sits near the bottom of the ladder, not the top.

## Ownership changes the conversation

I found it helpful to compare ownership models:

- **Utility-owned** — simpler to finance and coordinate, but benefits flow mainly through the utility.
- **Private developer with a community benefit agreement** — local payments or funds, but limited local control.
- **Co-operative or community-owned** — benefits and decisions stay local, but projects can be harder to finance.
- **Indigenous-owned or equity partnerships** — Indigenous nations owning or co-owning projects, which can support self-determination, revenue and long-term capacity.

The pattern I noticed: the more ownership and decision-making sit with the community, the more likely the project is to be seen as fair — and the more likely it is to be accepted. Community energy has been described as being about both *process* (who it is by) and *outcome* (who it is for). [[Add citation — e.g. Walker & Devine-Wright (2008)]]

## Questions I'm left with

- How can smaller communities access the capital they need to own projects, not just host them?
- What does meaningful participation look like when timelines are tight?
- How should recognition of Indigenous rights and knowledge be built into planning from day one?

## Key takeaways

> - "Clean" and "fair" are separate tests. Good projects aim to pass both.
> - Participation should shape decisions, not just inform people about them.
> - Ownership is one of the strongest levers for distributing benefits and building trust.

posts.title: The relevance of SDG 7 to local communities
posts.excerpt: SDG 7 is often talked about as a global target for other places. Looking closer, its promise of affordable, reliable, sustainable and modern energy is surprisingly local.
posts.body:
Sustainable Development Goal 7 aims to *"ensure access to affordable, reliable, sustainable and modern energy for all."* When I first read it, I filed it mentally under international development — something about electrification in other parts of the world. This week's readings made me realise how local it is.

## The targets, in plain language

- **7.1** — Everyone has access to affordable, reliable, modern energy services.
- **7.2** — A much larger share of energy comes from renewable sources.
- **7.3** — The rate of improvement in energy efficiency doubles.
- **7.a and 7.b** — Countries cooperate on research, investment and infrastructure, especially to support developing countries.

## Why it matters close to home

Even in wealthy countries, the four words *affordable, reliable, sustainable, modern* don't apply equally to everyone:

- **Affordable** — some households spend a large share of their income on heating and power. Energy poverty is real in cold climates.
- **Reliable** — rural and remote communities can face more frequent outages and longer restoration times.
- **Sustainable** — many remote communities in Canada are not connected to the main grid and still rely on diesel generators.
- **Modern** — older, poorly insulated homes lock people into high bills and discomfort.

Seen this way, SDG 7 isn't something that's "done" once a country has an electricity grid. It's a lens for asking who is still being left behind.

## What local action can look like

- Home energy retrofits targeted at households with the highest energy burden.
- Community-owned solar or wind projects that keep benefits local.
- Microgrids and storage to reduce diesel dependence in remote communities.
- Energy literacy programmes, so people can make informed choices.
- Local energy plans that connect housing, transport and economic development.

[[If relevant, add an example from your own community or home country here — local examples make this post much stronger.]]

## Key takeaways

> - SDG 7 is about everyone, everywhere — including communities in wealthy countries.
> - The four qualities in the goal give a practical checklist for local energy planning.
> - Local ownership and efficiency are two of the most direct ways to make progress.

*Sources to add: UN SDG 7 targets and indicators [[add link]]; Tracking SDG 7 report [[add year]].*

posts.title: Energy security and Canada's energy transition
posts.excerpt: For a major energy producer like Canada, energy security isn't only about keeping supply flowing. It's also about economic resilience, reliable grids and a transition that regions and workers can trust.
posts.body:
Most of the energy security writing I'd read before this programme came from the perspective of energy *importers*: countries worried about where their oil and gas would come from. Canada sits in a very different position, and that has made me rethink what energy security means.

## A producer's view of security

Canada is one of the world's major producers and exporters of energy, with large oil, natural gas, uranium and hydroelectric resources. For a country like this, energy security has several layers:

- **Supply security at home** — keeping homes heated and the lights on, especially through long, cold winters.
- **Economic security** — many communities, provincial budgets and jobs depend on energy production.
- **Security for partners** — the conversation about supplying allies has grown louder since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

One framing I found helpful from the readings defines energy security as the low vulnerability of vital energy systems. That shifts the question from "do we have enough?" to "what could disrupt the systems we depend on, and how exposed are we?" [[Add citation — e.g. Cherp & Jewell (2014)]]

## Why the transition changes the picture

Canada has committed in law to reaching net-zero emissions by 2050. Moving towards that goal changes where the vulnerabilities sit:

- **Electricity becomes more central.** As heating and transport electrify, grid reliability becomes a bigger part of energy security.
- **Provinces start from very different places.** Some generate most of their power from hydro; others, including Saskatchewan, have relied heavily on coal and natural gas. One national target means very different journeys.
- **Extreme weather tests the system.** Cold snaps, heat waves and wildfires put pressure on both supply and infrastructure.
- **New dependencies appear.** Critical minerals, supply chains for equipment and skilled workers become part of the security conversation.

## What I'm taking from this

I used to think of the transition and energy security as being in tension. I now think the more useful question is *how* a transition is managed. A rushed or poorly coordinated transition can create insecurity. A well-planned one — with stronger interties between provinces, storage, diverse supply and support for affected workers — can make the system more resilient than it is today.

## Key takeaways

> - Energy security for a producer country includes economic and regional security, not just supply.
> - The transition shifts vulnerabilities rather than simply adding or removing them.
> - Trust matters: regions and workers need to see a credible place for themselves in the future system.

## Still thinking about

How should provinces with very different energy mixes share the costs and benefits of a national transition? [[Add your own reflection or a local example from your coursework.]]

posts.title: Understanding the energy trilemma
posts.excerpt: Security, equity and environmental sustainability: why the energy trilemma is less a scorecard and more a set of questions worth asking about every energy decision.
posts.body:
When I first saw the phrase "energy trilemma" on a lecture slide, I assumed it was one of those tidy frameworks that look good in a diagram and fall apart in the real world. A few weeks in, I've changed my mind — at least partly.

## What the trilemma is

The World Energy Council describes energy systems as balancing three goals:

- **Energy security** — whether supply is reliable, and whether the system can withstand and recover from shocks.
- **Energy equity** — whether people and businesses can access energy and afford it.
- **Environmental sustainability** — the environmental footprint of the system, especially greenhouse gas emissions.

The point isn't that these three goals always conflict. It's that decisions which strengthen one often put pressure on another, and good policy makes those trade-offs visible instead of pretending they don't exist.

## A simple example that helped me

To make sense of it, I sketched out a simplified choice for a fictional province that needs new electricity supply:

- **Extend an old coal plant.** It feels secure in the short term and is affordable today, but it performs badly on emissions and carries growing policy and carbon-price risk.
- **Build a natural gas plant.** Flexible and lower-emitting than coal, but exposed to fuel price swings and likely to lock in infrastructure for decades.
- **Invest in wind, storage and stronger connections to neighbouring grids.** Low emissions and no fuel costs, but reliability depends on careful planning, and the upfront costs land on someone.

None of these options "wins" on all three dimensions. What changed my thinking was realising that the trilemma works best as a set of questions: *secure for whom? affordable for whom? sustainable over what timeframe?*

## Where I think the framework is limited

- **It can flatten justice into affordability.** Equity in the trilemma is mainly about access and price. The energy justice literature asks broader questions about who takes part in decisions and whose knowledge is recognised.
- **National scores hide local realities.** A country can perform well overall while some remote communities still depend on expensive, polluting diesel.
- **It can look static.** Real systems change. Today's trade-off can become tomorrow's synergy as costs fall and technologies mature.

## Key takeaways

> - The trilemma makes trade-offs visible; it doesn't resolve them for you.
> - Always ask *who* benefits from security, affordability and sustainability.
> - Pairing the trilemma with energy justice thinking captures participation and recognition, not just price.

## A question for readers

How should a jurisdiction weigh short-term affordability against long-term security when the costs of change fall unevenly? I'd genuinely like to hear how others think about this.

*Sources to add: World Energy Council, World Energy Trilemma Index [[add year and link]]; course readings [[add]].*

posts.title: First weeks in the programme: what I expected and what surprised me
posts.excerpt: I arrived expecting to learn mostly about technology. A few weeks in, the bigger lesson is that energy questions are really questions about people, institutions and trade-offs.
posts.body:
I've been meaning to start this journal since orientation, and I'm finally sitting down to write. Part of the reason for keeping it public is accountability — if I write things down where others can see them, I'm more likely to keep going.

## What I expected

I came into the Master of Sustainability expecting energy security to be mostly about supply: pipelines, power plants, reserves and the occasional geopolitical crisis. I assumed I'd spend most of my time learning the technical side of renewables and how grids work.

## What surprised me

The technical material is there, but what's struck me most so far is how *interdisciplinary* every conversation becomes. A discussion about a new transmission line turns out to be about land, treaty rights, consultation, prices, jobs and the climate — all at once. My classmates come from very different backgrounds, and I've already learned as much from their questions as from the readings.

I've also had to get comfortable with uncertainty. Many of the questions we're asked don't have a single correct answer. They have better and worse arguments, and the work is in explaining the trade-offs clearly.

## Things I'm going to try

- Writing one short reflection a week, even if it's rough.
- Keeping a reading log with a one-line summary of each source.
- Asking "secure for whom?" whenever I read about energy security.
- Being braver about sharing half-formed ideas — like this post.

## Key takeaways

> Energy questions are rarely only technical. The interesting part is usually in the trade-offs, and in who gets to decide.
